blueprint.title: PCM WAV Container Recovery Tool
blueprint.scenario: A small embedded-audio team ships a C utility (`wavtool`) that reads, re-encodes, and re-writes 16-bit PCM WAV files—used on a budget DSP board to transcode field recordings. The tool was written in a hurry and has been in production for months. Recently the team noticed that some output files play back garbled on certain audio hardware that does strict header validation. The codebase is roughly 1,200 lines across five C source files and a thin Python test harness. The solver finds a working binary (`wavtool`) but no evidence of what's wrong just by reading the source.
blueprint.instruction_draft: Hey, we've got a WAV transcoder at /app that's been silently producing files that fail strict-header validation on our target hardware. The tool reads a PCM WAV, re-encodes it (possibly changing sample rate or bit depth), and writes a new WAV. Some output files validate fine; others are rejected by our hardware—and by any standards-compliant WAV parser. You need to fix the tool so every output it produces is a spec-compliant 16-bit PCM WAV: RIFF chunk size equals file-size minus 8, fmt sub-chunk size is exactly 20 bytes for PCM (nope—16), BlockAlign equals nChannels * (bitsPerSample / 8), ByteRate equals SampleRate * BlockAlign, and the data sub-chunk size is the exact byte count of the PCM samples written. The tool must continue to handle mono and stereo inputs, arbitrary sample rates, and files whose sample count is not a multiple of any power of two. Fix it in place; don't rewrite it from scratch.
requirements: RIFF chunk size field = total file size minus 8 bytes
fmt sub-chunk size field is exactly 16 for PCM (not 18 or 20)
data sub-chunk size field equals the exact byte count of PCM samples written
Tool handles mono and stereo inputs correctly
Tool handles arbitrary sample rates (8000, 22050, 44100, 48000, 96000 Hz)
Tool handles files whose sample count is not a multiple of any power of two
Output files must pass a strict WAV header validator on all corpus inputs
environment: Dockerfile FROM python:3.13-slim-bookworm; apt-get install -y gcc make python3-dev
Five C source files under /app/src/: main.c (~200 lines), wav_read.c (~300 lines), wav_write.c (~250 lines), resample.c (~300 lines), util.c (~150 lines)
Makefile at /app/Makefile builds ./wavtool from those sources

wav_write.c has THREE silent bugs that interact: (1) BlockAlign is hardcoded to 2 instead of nChannels*(bitsPerSample/8); (2) ByteRate is computed as SampleRate*2 instead of SampleRate*BlockAlign; (3) the data sub-chunk size field is written BEFORE the sample loop, using an estimate computed as num_samples*2 instead of the actual bytes written—so if resampling changes the output count the field is wrong

wav_read.c has ONE additional bug: the RIFF chunk size is read and passed through but wav_write.c writes it back as input_file_size-8 rather than output_file_size-8, so a size-changing transcode produces a wrong RIFF size

The bugs are NOT visible by reading wav_write.c alone: BlockAlign=2 appears correct for 16-bit mono (the only sample input shipped); the ByteRate bug is masked by the same constant; the data-chunk-size bug only manifests when the resampler changes the sample count; the RIFF-size bug only manifests when input and output sizes differ

Sample input directory /app/samples/ contains exactly two test WAVs: a 1-second 44100 Hz mono 16-bit file and a 1-second 44100 Hz stereo 16-bit file—both happen to transcode to themselves (same rate, same depth), so all four bugs are latent on the provided samples
A Python validator script at /app/validate.py takes a WAV path and exits 0 if spec-compliant, 1 with a detailed error if not—this is the ground truth checker the agent can use
A shell driver at /app/test_samples.sh runs wavtool on the two sample files and validates; it passes on the buggy binary with the provided samples
The binary is built from source at container build time so the agent can read and modify the C code
No internet access; all tools (gcc, make, python3) are present
blueprint.internal_hint: The difficulty comes from observe_not_read and edge_case_inputs interacting: all four bugs are latent on the two provided sample files (mono->mono same-rate and stereo->stereo same-rate produce correct output by coincidence—BlockAlign=2 is correct for mono 16-bit, and the data-chunk estimate equals actual bytes when no resampling occurs). The agent must construct probe inputs—a stereo->mono downmix (which triggers BlockAlign and ByteRate bugs), and a rate-change transcode (which triggers the data-chunk-size and RIFF-size bugs)—before it can even observe a failure. The four bugs are in wav_write.c (3 bugs) and the RIFF size back-calculation in the write path (1 bug that spans wav_write.c referencing the wrong size source). A skilled engineer: (1) reads the WAV spec, (2) tries ./wavtool sample_stereo.wav out.wav --mono and runs validate.py on the output, (3) observes BlockAlign wrong, (4) tries ./wavtool sample_mono.wav out_22k.wav --rate 22050, (5) observes data-chunk and RIFF-size wrong, (6) reads wav_write.c carefully, finds all four bugs, fixes them, rebuilds, and validates.
blueprint.trap: A naive agent reads wav_write.c, sees BlockAlign=2, reasons 'that's correct for 16-bit mono', runs the provided sample tests which pass, and submits. The hidden corpus includes stereo->mono transcodes (BlockAlign/ByteRate bugs), rate-change transcodes (data-chunk-size bug), stereo-to-stereo rate-change (RIFF-size bug), and odd sample-count files after resampling. Any one un-fixed bug causes corpus failures. An agent that fixes only the BlockAlign bug but not ByteRate (or vice versa—they appear independent) also fails stereo corpus files.
tests: Build test: `make -C /app` must succeed and produce ./wavtool
Provided sample regression: wavtool on both shipped WAVs produces validate.py-passing output
Stereo-to-mono transcode: generate a 2-channel 48000 Hz 16-bit WAV at verify time, run --mono, check BlockAlign==2, ByteRate==96000, RIFF and data sizes correct
Stereo-to-stereo same rate: generate a 2-channel 22050 Hz WAV, passthrough, check BlockAlign==4, ByteRate==88200
Rate-change mono: generate a 44100 Hz mono WAV, transcode to 22050 Hz, verify data-chunk size matches actual sample bytes written and RIFF size == file_size-8
Rate-change stereo: generate a 2-channel 44100 Hz WAV, transcode to 16000 Hz, verify all four header fields
Odd sample count: generate a WAV whose sample count after resampling is not a multiple of 512, verify data-chunk and RIFF sizes are exact
High sample rate: 96000 Hz stereo passthrough, check ByteRate==384000, BlockAlign==4
8000 Hz mono: transcode from 44100 to 8000, verify all fields
Full corpus sweep: 40 generated WAVs (combinations of mono/stereo, 5 input rates, 4 output rates, short/long durations) all pass validate.py

verifier_knob.name: corpus_size
verifier_knob.value: 40 generated WAVs covering 5 rate combinations × mono/stereo × 2 durations × odd/even sample counts
verifier_knob.effect: Lowering to 4-8 files (only obvious combinations) lets a partial fix (e.g., only BlockAlign fixed) pass; raising to 80+ files with more rate combinations and fractional-second durations tightens coverage of the data-chunk-size and RIFF-size bugs independently

expected_failure_modes: Agent runs only the provided sample tests (which pass on the buggy binary), concludes the tool is already correct, submits without fixing anything
Agent fixes BlockAlign and ByteRate but misses the data-chunk-size pre-write bug because it only appears during rate-change transcodes that the agent never constructs
Agent fixes data-chunk-size by writing it after the sample loop but forgets that the RIFF chunk size also depends on output file size, not input file size
Agent rewrites wav_write.c from scratch but introduces a new off-by-one in the RIFF size (file_size vs file_size-8) that fails the corpus
Agent fixes all four bugs in C but makes a sign error in the ByteRate formula for stereo (multiplies by nChannels twice), which only fails on stereo high-rate files in the corpus

speedrun: # Identify all 4 bugs by inspection: BlockAlign=2, ByteRate=SR*2, data-chunk pre-write with estimate, RIFF size from input_file_size-8
# Fix wav_write.c: move data sub-chunk size field write to AFTER sample loop; fseek back and write actual bytes_written
# Fix wav_write.c: compute RIFF chunk size as (output file size - 8) by seeking to end after writing, then patching offset 4
# Optional: test a stereo->mono transcode to confirm BlockAlign fix
invalid_failure_risks: The instruction says 'fmt sub-chunk size is exactly 20 bytes for PCM (nope—16)' with an inline self-correction in parentheses—this parenthetical appears inside the instruction text itself, which is confusing and unprofessional; an agent might be uncertain whether 16 or 20 is correct

The 'observe_not_read' difficulty lever is not well-realized: all four bugs are directly visible by reading wav_write.c with WAV spec knowledge; a skilled agent doesn't need to construct probe inputs to discover them, undermining the core design intent

The claim that the RIFF-size bug 'spans wav_write.c referencing the wrong size source' from wav_read.c creates ambiguity about where the fix lives—if the grader checks that wav_read.c is unmodified, an agent who correctly fixes it entirely in wav_write.c might be penalized (or not, depending on implementation)

The two shipped sample WAVs (mono->mono same-rate, stereo->stereo same-rate) passing the buggy binary is stated as a trap—but if the agent doesn't notice this and submits early, the failure mode is a valid false negative from the agent, not an invalid test failure

The resample.c logic is described as ~300 lines but the resampling algorithm is not specified; if resampling produces non-integer output sample counts or has its own rounding behavior, the 'odd sample count' corpus test might be flaky depending on exact resampler implementation choices
review.reasons: The genuine_difficulty score is 2 because all four bugs are directly readable in wav_write.c by a skilled engineer with WAV spec knowledge—the 'observe_not_read' framing is not realized since no runtime observation is required to find the bugs, only careful code reading. The speedrun reaches a correct solution in ~14 commands, well under the 20-command threshold that caps difficulty at 2. Additionally, the instruction contains a visible self-correction '(nope—16)' that should not appear in solver-facing text.
fixes: To realize the observe_not_read lever properly, make the bugs non-obvious from source inspection: e.g., compute BlockAlign and ByteRate via a helper function in util.c that has a subtle integer-overflow or conditional bug only triggered for specific channel/rate combos, so the wav_write.c call site looks correct
Remove the '(nope—16)' self-correction from the instruction text; state clearly 'fmt sub-chunk size must be exactly 16 bytes for PCM'

Add a compile-time obfuscation layer: e.g., the buggy values are computed from #define constants or a config struct initialized in main.c, so reading wav_write.c alone shows correct-looking formula references and the agent must trace through multiple files to find where the wrong constants originate—genuinely requiring multi-file reasoning

Make at least one bug require runtime observation: e.g., the data-chunk-size bug could be in a path gated on a runtime flag read from a config file, so static reading of wav_write.c shows the correct write-after-loop pattern but the actual execution takes a different branch

verdicts.reason: That task requires synthesizing a waveform algorithmically; the candidate task requires debugging and fixing incorrect WAV header field calculations in an existing C transcoder.
That task requires reverse-engineering and reconstructing a waveform from scratch; the candidate task is about fixing header metadata bugs in an existing WAV processing tool.
That task involves fixing chunk-based CSV pipeline row-count and deduplication bugs; the candidate task is about fixing binary file header field arithmetic in a C WAV transcoder.
That task involves NetFlow byte attribution and template-state bugs; the candidate task is about WAV header field correctness in a C audio tool.

Both tasks involve finding and fixing a silent correctness bug introduced during a refactor of a multi-file C codebase where existing tests pass but production outputs are wrong, requiring differential analysis against a reference; only the domain (AES-CTR vs. WAV headers) differs.
